title: Looking back: the daily banis
hookLine: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, heard in order

cards: Six banis. One day. A Sikh home before dawn: a kettle, a dark window, a voice already reading.
By breakfast, several prayers have passed. At dusk, another. At bedtime, one more, with the lights low.
This year you met each of those prayers on its own, block by block, sometimes for weeks. Today you hear them as they're lived: in order, one day long. Looking back: the daily banis.

teach.b: Start in the dark. Amritvela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, is when the Sikh code of conduct asks a Sikh to rise, bathe and begin.

After the Japji comes the Jaap Sahib, which Sikhs know as Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise, all short lines and quick meters. You met its line in the spring: namastvam akaale, salutation to the One beyond time.
Then the Tav Prasad Savaiye, ten verses under the heading by Your grace: the poet has seen monks, yogis and mighty kings by the thousand, and says all of it is worth nothing without love.
Then, in some homes, the Benti Chaupai, a prayer for shelter: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa, give me Your hand and keep me safe.
Then Guru Amar Das's Anand Sahib, the song of bliss, which opens with a cry of joy: anand bhaiaa meree maae, I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. That's the morning.
Then the day itself: work, traffic, dishes, people. The banis don't ask anyone to leave it. They frame it.
At dusk, as work ends, Rehras, the evening prayer. It opens with So Dar, the door where the Creator sits and cares for all.
And last, at bedtime, Kirtan Sohila, five short hymns, beginning jai ghar keerat aakheeai: in the house where the Creator's praises are sung.
The same hymns are sung at funerals, so the close of a day and the close of a life share one song. Notice what the order does. Praise first, before anything has happened.
Shelter for the hours ahead. Joy. A door at dusk.

teach.h: NIGHT: SOHILA, THE SONG FOR SLEEP.

teach.b: The whole day, held between words.

how: Many Sikhs say the Japji, Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Savaiye in the early morning, often with Chaupai and Anand Sahib, then Rehras at dusk and Kirtan Sohila before sleep.

o: regretting the mistakes of the past year
reading the Granth from its last page first
seeing the year's daily banis side by side

games.q: the daily banis — tap the pairs.
p: salutation to the One beyond time
I am in bliss, O my mother

s: Kirtan Sohila is only ever said at bedtime
it is also sung at funerals: the close of a day and of a life share one song.
Rehras is said at dusk, as the day's work ends
it's the evening prayer, opening with So Dar, the door where the Creator sits.
the Savaiye say outward power counts for much even without love
they say the opposite: monks, yogis and kings are worth nothing without love.

games.q: the work is done and the light is going. which bani do many Sikhs say now?
games.why: Rehras is the dusk prayer; Jaap belongs to the morning, and Asa di Var is sung before sunrise.

practice: Say one line from each, slowly, aloud or under your breath, with a full breath between: namastvam akaale; tav prasad, by Your grace; hamree karo hath dai rachhaa; anand bhaiaa meree maae; so dar; jai ghar keerat aakheeai.
If a line won't come, say it in English, and let that be enough. Then rest in the quiet after the sixth.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Turning around near the top of the year to see the daily banis together: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, from before dawn to bedtime.

orig.note: Punjabi: the word of the Gurus, the hymns themselves; the daily banis are the ones said each day.

carryVoice: Your line: the day, held. Words at both edges, and the day between. Until tomorrow.
